_about: Concept ladder for the Learn stage. One concept per rung. Rung ids are progress keys: never rename. skills are glossary.json ids that move to Practiced when the check is passed. goals maps checkpoint data-ids to the rungs (1-based) that teach them. lang: c programs are compiled and run to verify each check.

rungs.title: Name the function signature in your prompt
rungs.builds: Phase 3: functions, parameters and return values. Phase 3.5: the Player struct.
rungs.why: Claude fills every gap in your prompt with a guess. A guess that compiles looks right until it doesn’t match your code. Writing the signature yourself, the way you’d write a function prototype, closes the biggest gap before any code exists.
rungs.model: Mental model: ordering at a counter. “Something with chicken” gets you anything. “A small chicken wrap, no mayo” gets you what you wanted. The signature is the order.

check.q: You want a jump function for your ASCII runner. Which prompt is most likely to give you exactly that?
opts: Add jumping to my runner game. Make it feel good and handle everything it needs.
Write int player_jump(Player p) that makes the player jump when they’re on the ground.
Write void player_jump(Player *p): if p->y is 0, set p->vy to 3. Only this function, no new structs.
I’m making a runner in C. Write all the movement code: jump, duck, gravity and collision.
check.hint: Which prompt tells Claude what the function takes, what it does, and where it stops?
check.why: The third prompt fixes the signature, the number and the scope. There’s almost nothing left to guess, and you can check the answer against your own words.

miss.0: “Feel good” and “everything it needs” hand all the decisions to Claude. You’ll get its design, not yours.
miss.1: It names a signature, but with the wrong details: it returns an int you didn’t ask for and takes a copy of the Player, so a jump would never reach your real one. It also leaves “jump” and the height for Claude to guess.
miss.3: Four systems in one prompt means a pile of code you didn’t design and can’t review in one sitting. Ask for one function at a time.

tryit.task: Fill the blanks so this prompt names the signature and fences the scope.
tryit.code:
I’m building a guessing game in C.
Write ____ check_guess(int guess, int secret).
It returns -1 if guess is below secret, 1 if above, 0 if equal.
Write only this function. Don’t add ____ or ____.
tryit.answer: int (the return type). Then any two things you don’t want, for example: printf calls, scanf input, new structs, other functions.

qa: Do I have to know the answer before I ask?
You need to know the shape: name, inputs, output. That’s a design decision, and it’s yours. Claude writes the body.
What if I’m not sure what the parameters should be?
Ask Claude to critique your plan first (the “is my approach right?” template), then write the signature yourself.
Isn’t this just writing the code myself?
It’s writing the one line that matters. The signature is the contract. The body is detail you can check against it.
What happens to the parts I leave out of a prompt?

Claude fills every gap with a guess, and a guess that compiles looks right until it doesn’t match your structs or your partner’s code. Paste your structs and existing function names first, then ask for one thing.
rungs.bridge: You can pin down what you want. Next: reading every line of what comes back, before you run it.
rungs.code:
Vague prompt:
  Make the player jump.

Better prompt:
  I’m building an ASCII runner in C. My Player struct has int y and int vy.
  Write void player_jump(Player *p). If p->y is 0 (on the ground), set p->vy to 3. Otherwise do nothing.
  Write only this function. No new structs, no new files.
walk: Claude has to guess everything here: the name, what it takes, what it returns, what “jump” means in numbers. Every guess is a place the code can come out wrong.
Context first: the language, the game, and the fields that already exist. Claude can use your y and vy instead of inventing its own.

The signature: return type, name, parameters. You learned in Phase 3 that this one line fixes how the function is called. If you write it, you’ll notice straight away if Claude’s code doesn’t match it. Player *p is a pointer to your real Player, and p->y reaches a field through it (both from Phase 3.5).
The exact behaviour, with exact numbers. “On the ground” is turned into a test Claude can code.
The fence. Without it you often get three helper functions and a new struct you never asked for.

parts: Gaps become guesses

Claude can't see what's in your head. Every detail you leave out of a prompt, it fills with the most likely guess. Most guesses compile, which is the trouble: code that builds but takes a copy of your Player instead of a pointer looks fine until the jump never happens. The fix is to close the gaps before any code exists, and the biggest gap is the function's shape.
Four parts of a tight prompt

1. Context. The language, the game, and the structs or functions that already exist. Paste them, or name the file: Claude Code can read your project, so “my Player struct in player.h” works.
  2. The signature. Return type, name and parameters, written exactly as a prototype: void player_jump(Player *p).
  3. The behaviour, with numbers. “If p->y is 0, set p->vy to 3” instead of “make it jump nicely”.
  4. The fence. What not to touch: “Only this function. No new structs, no new files.”
Why the signature matters most

The signature is the contract between the function and every line that calls it. You learned in void and function prototypes that this one line decides what goes in and what comes out. If you write it, you can check Claude's answer in two seconds: does the first line match yours? If it says int where you wrote void, or Player p where you wrote Player *p, you know something else was guessed too.
Mistakes that cost you

• Asking for a system (“all the movement code”) instead of one function. You get a pile you can't review.
  • Taste words like “clean”, “good” or “feel nice”. They mean nothing to a compiler.
  • Forgetting the pointer. A function that changes your struct needs Player *, as in Passing by pointer.
  • Leaving out existing names, so Claude invents playerY when you already have p->y.
Your build flags still apply
Tell Claude you build with MSVC cl /std:c17 /W4 /WX. Otherwise it may use things that fail under your flags, such as a variable it never uses, or a GCC-only feature.
learn.king: §9.1–9.2 (defining functions and prototypes), if you want the C side again

rungs.title: Read every line before you run it
rungs.builds: Phase 3: the high-score table, arrays and loops. Name the function signature in your prompt: asking for exact functions.
rungs.why: Code that compiles and looks tidy can still be wrong. Your name is on the commit, and an out-of-bounds write may print fine today and crash next week. The only defence is reading each line and tracing it with a real number.
rungs.model: Mental model: proofreading a contract before you sign. The font is nice and every sentence sounds fine, but you’re the one who’s bound by it.

check.q: Claude’s add_score builds with no warnings under /W4 /WX. Which line should you question before you run it?
opts: for (int j = 5; j > i; j--)
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
table[i] = score;
return;
check.hint: Count the slots, then check where the first shift writes.
check.why: Valid indexes are 0 to 4. With j starting at 5, the first shift writes table[5], past the end of the array. The compiler can’t see it. Trace it with a small table and you’ll spot it.

miss.1: Looks right, and it is: i < 5 visits indexes 0 to 4. The bug is elsewhere.
miss.2: Once the gap is open, putting the score at index i is right.
miss.3: return stops after one insert so the score isn’t added twice. That’s needed.

tryit.task: Fix the one line so the shift stays inside the array.
tryit.answer: 4. The last valid index of a 5-slot array.

qa: It compiled with no warnings. Isn’t that proof?
No. The compiler checks grammar, not meaning. An out-of-bounds write compiles, but it’s undefined behaviour: C doesn’t check it, so anything can happen.
How do I check code I can’t follow?
Pick a small real input, like a table of 50 40 30 20 10 and a score of 45, and step through with a pencil. Ask for explanations of code you don't understand covers the parts you can't trace.
Should I read the code even for tiny functions?
Yes, those are the quickest to read. The habit matters more than the size.
rungs.bridge: You can catch a bad line. Next: asking for explanations when a line is something you don’t recognise yet.
walk: The signature matches what you asked for. Good start, but a right signature doesn’t mean a right body.
The outer loop walks the five slots, 0 to 4. Check the bounds: i < 5 stops at index 4. Fine.
Finds the first entry the new score beats. Because the table is sorted, that’s the right place to insert.
Question this line. The table has indexes 0 to 4. This starts at j = 5, so the next line writes table[5], one past the end. It should start at 4.
Shifts entries down to make room. With j = 5 this writes outside the array. C won’t stop you.
Drops the new score into the gap. This part is right.

parts: Compiling isn't checking

The compiler checks that code is legal C. It doesn't check that it does what you asked. An off-by-one loop, a missing bounds check or a wrong number all build cleanly under /W4 /WX. Your name goes on the commit, and Person A will trust it, so every line gets read before it runs.
Trace it with a real number

Reading isn't skimming. Pick a small, real input and follow it through by hand:

  1. Write the input on paper: a table of 50 40 30 20 10 and a new score of 45.
  2. Go line by line. Each time a variable changes, write its new value.
  3. At every array access, write the index you're about to use and check it's inside the array.
  4. Check the result matches what you asked for in the prompt.

Then try an edge case: the lowest score, the highest, an empty table. Bugs live at the edges.
What to look at hardest

• Loop bounds. Does the first and last pass touch a valid index? An array of 5 has indexes 0 to 4.
  • Every index and pointer. Where does it point on the first pass and the last?
  • Return values. Is the result of fopen, malloc or scanf checked?
  • Casts. A cast can hide a real problem just to silence a warning.
  • Anything you don't recognise. That's a question for Ask for explanations of code you don't understand, not something to skip.
Why “it ran fine” proves little

Writing past the end of an array is undefined behaviour. C doesn't check, so the program might print the right answer, crash later somewhere else, or quietly change a neighbouring variable. Running once and seeing good output tells you that one run worked. Tracing tells you why.
Let the debugger help
For a loop you can't trace on paper, set a breakpoint and step through it in the debugger, watching the index in the Locals panel. Seeing j hit 5 on a five-slot array is hard to argue with.
learn.king: Not in King: this is a habit, not a C feature

rungs.title: Ask for explanations of code you don’t understand
rungs.kick: explain first · pick the edge case · then decide
rungs.builds: Read every line before you run it. Phase 3.5: addresses with &.
rungs.why: Claude will happily use functions you’ve never met. Running code you can’t explain is how bugs get into the project and stay there. A good question costs one message and turns a mystery line into something you own.
rungs.model: Mental model: a mechanic who shows you the old part. You don’t need to rebuild the engine, but you want to hear what broke and why before you pay.

check.q: Claude’s code uses memmove, which you’ve never seen. What do you send back?
opts: Looks fine to me, so I’m running it now.
Rewrite the whole function without memmove, using only things I’ve already learned.
Explain the whole add_score function to me from the very start.
Explain the memmove line and what happens when i is 4.
check.hint: Which reply is about the exact line you’re stuck on and gives you something to check?
check.why: A targeted question gets a targeted answer. You learn memmove, and you can test the “i is 4” answer yourself. You stay in charge of what goes in.

miss.0: You’d be running a line you can’t explain. That’s the habit this rung is about breaking.
miss.1: You throw away working code and learn nothing about memmove. Sometimes simpler is right (Push back when code is overcomplicated), but ask for that on purpose, not as a reflex.
miss.2: Too broad. You’ll get a long answer and still not know the one line you asked about.

tryit.task: Write the follow-up question. Name the line, the thing you don’t know, and a case to test.
tryit.code:
Explain the line ____ in add_score.
What does ____ mean there?
What happens when ____?
tryit.answer: For example: memmove(...), the third argument (4 - i) * sizeof(int), i is 0.

qa: Won’t asking questions make me look like I don’t know C?
The only person looking is you. Asking is how you learn it, and you’re the one who has to maintain this code.
How do I know the explanation is right?
Test it. Write a tiny program with a 5-slot table and run it. If the output matches the explanation, you’re set.
Should I ask for explanations every time?
Every time there’s a line you couldn’t explain to someone else. Familiar code, skip it.
rungs.bridge: You can get a line explained. Next: pushing back when the answer is more than you asked for.
walk: Three questions in one prompt: what it does, one edge case you choose (i is 4), and what could break. Picking the edge case yourself makes the answer concrete.
memmove is new to you. It copies a block of memory from one place to another, and it’s safe when the two blocks overlap. Here it replaces the inner shift loop.
First argument: where to copy to, the slot after i. The & means “the address of” (Phase 3.5).
Second argument: where to copy from, slot i itself.
Third argument: how many bytes to copy. (4 - i) is the number of entries that move, and sizeof(int) turns that into bytes. When i is 4, nothing moves.

parts: Own every line

Claude knows the whole C library and will use any of it. Sooner or later it hands you a line with a function you've never met. Running code you can't explain means the project has a part nobody understands. One focused question fixes that, and it usually takes a minute.
A question that gets a useful answer

Good follow-ups have three parts:

  1. The exact line. Paste it, so there's no doubt which one you mean.
  2. The part you don't know. “What is the third argument?” beats “what does this do?”.
  3. A case to test. “What happens when i is 4?” gives you an answer you can check.

Adding “what could go wrong with this line?” often turns up the edge case you hadn't thought of.
Check the explanation

Explanations can be wrong too. Test the claim with a tiny program: a five-slot table, the line in question, and a printf loop to show the result. If the output matches what Claude said, you've learned it for real. If not, paste the output back and ask why. Microsoft Learn's page for any C library function is a good second opinion.
Mistakes to avoid

• Asking for an explanation of the whole function when one line is the problem. The answer you need gets buried.
  • Asking for a rewrite with “only things I know” as a reflex. Sometimes simpler is right, as in Push back when code is overcomplicated, but ask for it on purpose.
  • Nodding along to an answer you didn't follow. Ask again in different words, or ask for a smaller example.
Keep a list

Each new function you learn this way, add to your notes with one line of your own words and a tiny example. The Things Claude may show you box on this phase's overview covers three that turn up often: memmove, malloc and free, and function-pointer typedefs.
learn.king: §23.6 for memmove and the other memory functions in string.h

rungs.title: Push back when code is overcomplicated
rungs.kick: simplify · “I don’t need X yet” · smallest thing that works
rungs.builds: Phase 3: functions and return values, the guessing game. Phase 3.75: function pointers. Read every line before you run it.
rungs.why: Claude tends to build for needs you haven’t got. Extra structs, allocation and callbacks look professional but give you more to read, more to break and more you don’t understand. You can tell it to cut them, and it will.
rungs.model: Mental model: asking for a bike and being handed a motorcycle. It does the job and more, but you have to learn the engine just to get to the shops.

check.q: You asked for check_guess and got the struct-and-callback version above. What do you say back?
opts: Great, I’ll learn from it and move on to the next function.
Simplify: int check_guess(guess, secret) returning -1, 0 or 1.
This is all wrong, so start from scratch and do it properly this time.
Add comments explaining each part so I can follow how it all works.
check.hint: Which reply names what to remove and what you want instead?
check.why: Naming the signature and the things to cut gives Claude a clear target. You end up with code you can read, and you remember that the complexity was optional.

miss.0: Accepting more than you asked for means owning code you don’t need. Features you don’t need still have bugs.
miss.2: “Do it properly” leaves the same gaps that caused this. Claude will guess again, maybe worse.
miss.3: Comments make the extra code easier to read, but it’s still extra. You asked for less, not for it to be explained.

tryit.task: Write the push-back. Name the signature to keep and two things to remove.
tryit.code:
Simplify this. I only need ____.
Remove the ____ and the ____. I don’t need them yet.
tryit.answer: For example: int check_guess(int guess, int secret). Then the struct and the callback (or malloc, or the enum).

qa: What if I might need the callback later?
Then add it later, when you do. Code is easy to extend and hard to untangle. “I don’t need X yet” is a complete reason.
How do I know it’s overcomplicated?
If you can't say in one sentence what each piece is for, or it uses things you haven't met yet (like malloc), push back. The Things Claude may show you box explains the common ones.
Will Claude be offended?
No. “Simplify” is a normal instruction and it works well.
How do I stop Claude rewriting my whole file?
Say show me ONLY the lines to add and where they go, and alongside the existing if you want an addition, not a replacement. You get a small diff you can read.
rungs.bridge: You can cut code down to size. Next: owning the architecture, deciding the shape of the game before Claude writes any of it.
walk: A vague prompt (see Name the function signature in your prompt) is how this happens. Claude guessed you wanted something “extensible”.
An enum you didn’t ask for. Something else to read and keep consistent.
A function pointer type (you met these in Phase 3.75) for a callback: a function to call later. Nothing here needs one.
A struct to wrap the result, also not asked for.
malloc hands you memory you now have to free later. Forget and the game leaks. For comparing two ints, that’s a heavy price.
The -> arrow reaches a field through a pointer (Phase 3.5). It’s only needed because the result lives in allocated memory.
A callback that fires from inside the function. Now check_guess has a side effect, and the order things happen in is harder to follow.
The same job in three lines. No allocation, no new types. You can read it in one pass and you already know every piece.

parts: More code is more risk

Ask a vague question and Claude often builds for needs you don't have yet: a struct for the result, an enum for three outcomes, a callback “for flexibility”, memory from malloc. Each piece is something you have to read, test and keep working. Code you don't need still has bugs, so asking for less is a normal, sensible request.
Signs it's overbuilt

• You can't say in one sentence what a piece is for.
  • malloc for something small with a fixed size, where a local variable or array would do.
  • New types or files you didn't ask for.
  • A function pointer passed in when there's only ever one thing to call.
  • The answer is three times longer than the job sounds.
How to push back

Be as specific as your first prompt should have been:

  1. Name what to keep: the exact signature you want.
  2. Name what to remove: “no struct, no callback, no malloc”.
  3. Give the reason in four words: “I don't need X yet”.

“Do it properly” or “that's wrong” leave the same gaps, so you'll get another guess. To stop it rewriting a whole file, ask it to show only the lines to add and where they go.
When the extra is right

Sometimes the bigger version is the right call: a buffer whose size comes from a level file really does need malloc. If you're not sure, ask “why did you use malloc here, and what would break with a plain array?” before you cut it. Then decide. The choice should be yours, made on purpose.
Watch for leaks

If you keep a malloc, find the matching free before you accept the code. A function that allocates every frame and never frees will slowly eat memory while the game runs, and nothing warns you at build time.
learn.king: §17.1 and §17.4 (malloc and free), §17.7 (function pointers), to read about what you're cutting

rungs.title: Design the structs and prototypes first
rungs.kick: design first · prototypes as a plan · one piece at a time
rungs.builds: Phase 3.5: structs. Phase 4.5: the ASCII runner. Every earlier concept in this phase.
rungs.why: Claude can write code quickly, but the design is your job. If it picks the structs and the function list, you maintain a design you don’t understand. If you pick them, every piece it writes fits a plan you can explain.
rungs.model: Mental model: you’re the architect with the blueprint, Claude is the builder. A builder will happily improvise a house. It just won’t be the house you wanted.

check.q: You want to build the ASCII runner with Claude Code. What do you do first?
opts: Ask: build me an ASCII runner game in C.
Ask Claude to design the structs and every function, then accept it.
Write the structs and prototypes yourself, then ask for one function.
Ask for all the functions in one prompt so they match each other.
check.hint: Who should decide what the Player struct contains and which functions exist?
check.why: The design is yours. Prototypes are a plan you can read, and asking for one function at a time keeps each reply small enough to check line by line.

miss.0: Claude will pick the design for you, including things you won’t understand. You’ll own code you can’t explain.
miss.1: It’s fine to ask Claude to critique your plan. Handing the plan over entirely isn’t. You’d still be taking its design on trust.
miss.3: One huge reply is too much to read properly (see Read every line before you run it). Pieces that match come from your shared design, not from asking for everything at once.

tryit.task: Write one prototype for your runner’s design, and the scope line of the prompt that asks for it.
tryit.code:
bool ____(const Player *p, const Obstacle *o);

Prompt: Here are my structs and prototypes. Write only ____.
tryit.answer: For example: hits_obstacle, then “hits_obstacle”. The name in the prototype and in the prompt must match.

qa: Can I ask Claude for ideas on the design?
Yes. Use the “is my approach right?” template: describe your plan and ask for a critique, with no code yet. You decide what to keep.
What if my design turns out wrong?
Then change it, and you’ll know why. That’s better than finding out a design you never chose has a problem.
Do I redo this for every feature?
Yes, in small. A new feature gets a few lines of design (the struct field, the prototype) before the prompt.
rungs.bridge: That’s every concept in Phase 7. Next: keep using these habits in every phase from here. The goal is code you can explain.
walk: You wrote this part, not Claude. It took ten minutes and it’s the part that decides how the whole game fits together.
In C17 the name bool (and true, false) comes from <stdbool.h>. Leave this out and MSVC stops at the first bool.
Your data. Every function Claude writes will use these exact fields, so nothing is invented.

The list of jobs, as prototypes (Phase 3). The * parameters are pointers (Phase 3.5): the function works on your real Player, not a copy. Each is small enough to ask for on its own and to check on its own.
Even the return types are your decisions. A yes/no question returns bool. const promises the function only looks at the Player and Obstacle and won’t change them (Phase 4.5 covers const pointers).
One piece at a time, with your design pasted in as context. Claude fills in a body that has to fit your pieces.

parts: The design is your job

Claude writes code quickly. Deciding what the code should be is slower, and it's yours. If Claude picks the structs and the list of functions, you end up maintaining a design you didn't choose and can't fully explain. If you pick them, every piece Claude writes has to fit a plan you understand.
What “the design” means in C

For a small game, the design is just two things:

  • The structs. What data exists and what each field means: Player has x, y, vy and alive.
  • The prototypes. Every function's name, inputs and output, with const on pointers it only reads.

Written in a header, that's ten or twenty lines. It's the same split you used in Header files and #pragma once, and again in Multiple files and LNK2005: the .h says what exists, the .c files hold the bodies.
Working one piece at a time

1. Write the structs and prototypes yourself.
  2. Optionally, ask Claude to critique the plan, with no code yet. Keep the suggestions you understand and agree with.
  3. Ask for one function, pasting the design as context.
  4. Read it, build it, test it, commit it.
  5. Then the next function.

Each reply stays small enough to read line by line, and because they all use your structs, the pieces fit together.
Write your rules down once

Claude Code reads a file called CLAUDE.md in your project folder at the start of a session. Put your standing rules there: build with cl /std:c17 /W4 /WX, snake_case names, include <stdbool.h> for bool, one function per request. Then you don't repeat them in every prompt.
The bool include

In C17, bool, true and false come from <stdbool.h>. Leave the include out and MSVC stops at the first bool as an unknown name. C23 makes bool a keyword, so you'll see newer code without the include; your build isn't C23.
learn.king: §19.1–19.2 (modules and information hiding), the same idea at the size of a file
